title: The herb garden
hookLine: Guru Har Rai keeps a garden of medicines and sends a cure even to the emperor's son Dara Shikoh

lines: A SICK MAN FROM THE OTHER SIDE.
cards: Someone from a family that has hurt yours gets sick. Not a stranger: the grandson of the man who ordered your great-grandfather's death, the son of the ruler whose soldiers fought your grandfather.
His messengers come to your door. He's dying, and word is you have the medicine that could save him. Nobody would blame you for saying no.
Plenty of people would blame you for saying yes. That was the choice in front of Guru Har Rai, the gentle seventh Guru.

teach.b: At Kiratpur, Guru Har Rai kept a large garden of medicinal herbs, and a place where medicines were made and given out free.
Healing was part of his gentleness: the boy who wouldn't break a flower grew into a man who used plants to mend people.

The emperor Shah Jahan had a favorite son, Prince Dara Shikoh, the eldest, a scholar who loved the mystics of every tradition. Tradition says Dara fell dangerously ill, and the court physicians could find nothing to help.
Word came that a rare remedy was kept in the Guru's store, and the emperor sent a request.
This was the same royal family whose emperor Jahangir had ordered Guru Arjan's death, and whose forces had fought Guru Hargobind. The Guru sent the medicine, and tradition says Dara recovered.
Tradition gives the Guru's reason in a picture: a tree does not ask who is throwing stones at it before it gives fruit, and it gives shade to the one who cuts it down. Heal whoever asks.
Look back over the week: Guru Arjan, the first martyr, remembered with cold water for strangers. Two swords and a timeless throne.
A cloak that freed fifty-two. A Guru who knew when to rest.
A boy careful of flowers. And now a garden that heals the enemy's son. The thread is strength that won't turn bitter, and the Sikh story keeps saying it, week after week.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai for his herb garden and free medicines at Kiratpur, and many gurdwaras today run free clinics and medical camps in the same spirit of seva.

o: the emperor's eldest son, healed by the Guru
a court physician to the Mughal emperor
a Mughal general who fought Guru Hargobind

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the emperor who asked for help
gives shade even to the axe

s: the Guru refused to help the emperor's family
tradition says he sent the medicine, and Dara recovered.
medicines were given out free at Kiratpur
healing was part of the seventh Guru's gentleness.
Dara Shikoh was a scholar who loved the mystics
the emperor's eldest son was known for his interest in the mystics of many traditions.

games.q: you're Guru Har Rai. the son of the dynasty that killed your great-grandfather is dying, and asks for your medicine. what do you do?
o: send it only if the emperor apologizes.
games.why: tradition says he sent the cure: a tree gives shade even to the one who cuts it down.

practice: If there's a plant near you, go to it: water it, turn it toward the light, take off one dead leaf.

If there isn't, picture one you know, a tree on your street, something on a windowsill, and look at it the way a gardener does, noticing what it needs. Then sit with it a while and breathe: something alive, being looked after.

wordCard.voice: Dara Shikoh. The emperor's favorite son whom Guru Har Rai healed with medicine from his garden at Kiratpur, tradition says.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, from Persian: a dispensary, the house of medicines.

carryVoice: Your line: heal whoever asks. Tomorrow, a new week and a changed word. Day seventy, and another week complete.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition on Guru Har Rai's herb garden (dawakhana) at Kiratpur and the cure sent to Dara Shikoh
